narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 65% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but it was high enough to drive the rejection.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile. Your value of 2 is well below the average of about 5.79 among applicants who were accepted, and this was the top influence pushing the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your LSAT score of 38, slightly above the accepted average of 37.18, was the second most important factor and pushed toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40, also above the accepted average of 3.23, similarly pushed toward passing. However, those two positive signals ranked below your third-year class rank and were not enough to offset it.

Your next step should be to strengthen the academic part of your record that raised concern, especially the third-year decline. Consider additional coursework or a graduate-level program to show renewed performance, and seek a pre-law advisor to help explain any context behind the lower rank. Retake the LSAT only if practice tests suggest a meaningful improvement. Reapplying to a realistic range of schools, with a stronger recent academic record and a clear explanation of your trajectory, would be the most practical path.
